summary: Gives procedures for registering extensible parts of LDAP, such as attributes and object classes, and tells IANA under which conditions new values can be assigned. It is a best current practice and was replaced by RFC 4520.

plainLanguage.summary: When many people add new things to a shared list, someone needs rules for who can add what. This document gives those rules for LDAP.

questions: how to register ldap extensions with iana
what are the iana rules for ldap
subtitle: Rules for registering new LDAP extensions, attributes, and protocol elements with IANA.

tldr.problem: LDAP is an extensible protocol that supports new operations, extensions to existing operations, and extensible schema. These extensions require unique identifiers (Object Identifiers, descriptors, message types, and result codes). Without clear registration procedures and policies, duplicates could be assigned, breaking interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines registration procedures and policies (Standards Action, Expert Review, First Come First Served) for each extensible element: OIDs, protocol mechanisms, descriptors, attribute options, message types, result codes, and authentication methods. It specifies which policy applies to which range of values and how to apply.
tldr.outcome: IANA can maintain authoritative registries of LDAP extensions and assign new values using consistent, documented procedures. Organizations developing LDAP extensions know exactly what policy applies and how to register their work.

today: RFC 4520 obsoleted this document in 2006 with updated IANA considerations for LDAP. RFC 3383 remains historically important as the first standardized set of LDAP registration procedures, but implementors and those registering LDAP extensions should consult RFC 4520 for current guidance.

sections.title: LDAP Extensibility and Registration
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a directory protocol that supports three kinds of extensibility: addition of new operations, extension of existing operations, and extensible schema. These extensible elements include LDAP message types, extended operations and controls, result codes, authentication methods, attribute description options, and Object Identifier descriptors. Each extensible element is identified by an Object Identifier (OID)—a dotted numeric string like 1.3.6.1.1.5—or a short descriptive name (descriptor). To prevent duplicate assignments, LDAP protocol extensions and schema elements must be registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

The RFC serves as a Best Current Practice document, establishing registration procedures and policies that IANA uses when assigning new values. It provides procedures for registering each type of extensible element, guidelines for IANA on when and how to assign new values, and templates that registration requesters must use when submitting requests. By documenting these procedures, the RFC ensures that LDAP can evolve safely: new extensions can be deployed, interoperability is maintained across vendors, and the assignments remain stable and publicly available.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP lets developers add new features by assigning them new numbers. This document tells developers how to ask IANA for a number and tells IANA when to give one out.

sections.title: Extensible Elements and Identifiers
sections.content:
LDAP defines several kinds of extensible elements, each identified in different ways. Object Identifiers (OIDs) are dotted numeric strings used to identify LDAP schema and protocol elements. For IETF-developed elements, OIDs should be under the Internet Directory Numbers arc (1.3.6.1.1.x), assigned upon Expert Review with Specification Required. Elements developed by others can use any properly delegated OID, including those under Internet Private Enterprise Numbers (1.3.6.1.4.1.x). Experimental OIDs under the Internet Experimental OID arc (1.3.6.1.3.x) should be used in works in progress and early implementations but never in published specifications.

Object Identifier Descriptors are short names used instead of numeric OIDs to identify protocol extensions, schema elements, LDAP URLs, and other objects. Descriptors are case-insensitive and should be short (under 48 characters). Multiple names can be assigned to the same OID. Descriptors beginning with 'x-' are reserved for Private Use and cannot be registered. Descriptors beginning with 'e-' are reserved for experiments and registered on a First Come First Served basis. All other descriptors require Expert Review. A descriptor ending with a hyphen reserves all descriptors starting with that value, allowing families of related extensions.

AttributeDescription Options are strings within an AttributeDescription that specify additional semantics, case-insensitive and limited by length (under 24 characters is preferred). Like descriptors, options beginning with 'x-' are for Private Use, 'e-' are for experiments, and others require Standards Action or Expert Review. LDAP Message Types are identified by keywords and choice numbers, with new values requiring Standards Action. LDAP Result Codes are enumerated integers where values 0-1023 require Standards Action, 1024-4095 require Expert Review, and 4096-16383 are First Come First Served. LDAP Authentication Methods follow similar numeric policies and must be classified as COMMON, LIMITED USE, or OBSOLETE.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers, names, and classifications are used to identify different parts of LDAP. Different ranges have different approval rules to balance stability with flexibility.

sections.title: Registration Policies and Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC establishes four primary registration policies. Standards Action is the most restrictive: only IETF standards track RFCs can register values. Expert Review with Specification Required requires a public review period (two weeks) on the directory@apps.ietf.org mailing list, with an appointed Expert reviewing comments and approving or denying the request. First Come First Served is the most permissive: requesters submit directly to IANA with minimal review. Private Use allows any use without registration (descriptors and options beginning with 'x-', values in high numeric ranges). Different ranges of values for result codes, authentication methods, and options have different policies assigned to them. For example, result code values 0-1023 use Standards Action (high stability), 1024-4095 use Expert Review (medium), and 4096-16383 use First Come First Served (maximum flexibility).

Registration requesters must use provided templates specifying the element being registered, OID or numeric value, contact information, usage (where applicable), specification reference, author/change controller, and comments. For elements requiring Expert Review, the requester posts the form to the mailing list. For First Come First Served, the form is submitted directly to IANA. The requester is considered the owner of values they register, with rights to update them subject to the same constraints as new registrations. When registration ownership is disputed or changes are needed but the owner is unwilling, the IESG may assert ownership to update the registration. Comments from others may be attached to a registration upon Expert Review if significant objections to claims are raised and the owner does not agree to change the registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Some numbers need approval from the big committees (Standards Action), some need a public check (Expert Review), and some you can just grab if nobody took it (First Come First Served).

sections.title: Protocol Mechanisms and Schema Elements
sections.content:
Protocol Mechanisms include controls and extended operations, discovered through Root DSE attributes (supportedControl and supportedExtension). OIDs associated with discoverable protocol mechanisms should be registered on a First Come First Served with Specification Required basis. OIDs for Standard Track mechanisms must be registered and require Standards Action. This allows implementors and others to locate the technical specification for protocol mechanisms by consulting the IANA registry.

Schema Elements such as attributes and object classes are central to LDAP's extensibility. While the RFC does not define separate registration procedures for schema elements themselves, it establishes that schema elements are identified by OIDs and descriptors that follow the registration rules above. Schema developers define their attributes, object classes, and syntaxes using OIDs and descriptors, then register those identifiers with IANA. The RFC also notes that Directory Systems Names—a historical registry of LDAPv2 distinguished name keywords—will no longer accept new registrations. The current list is kept for historical purposes but has been superseded by LDAPv3's use of Object Identifier Descriptors. This transition reflects the evolution of LDAP from v2 to v3 and shows how LDAP registration procedures have matured over time.
sections.plainLanguage: New LDAP features are defined using numbers and names. The registry tells you how to ask for new numbers and who needs to approve them.

sections.title: Practical Guidance for Developers and IANA
sections.content:
For developers extending LDAP, the RFC provides practical guidance. Use OIDs under the Internet Directory Numbers arc for IETF-developed elements and proper delegations for others. Use experimental OIDs (1.3.6.1.3.x) in works in progress, never in published RFCs. Register all OIDs associated with Standard Track protocol mechanisms. For schema elements that should be broadly deployed, use Standards Action if you want maximal stability, or Expert Review if you want expert guidance with faster turnaround. For experimental features, use the 'e-' prefix for descriptors and 4096-16383 range for result codes and authentication methods, which use First Come First Served. For internal or proprietary extensions, use 'x-' prefix, which requires no registration.

For IANA, the RFC specifies that the Authority may reject obviously bogus registration requests. IANA maintains registries publicly on its website and uses the specified policies to assign values. The RFC establishes that registration owners maintain control of their entries but the IESG may assert ownership when updates are necessary and owners are unable or unwilling. The registries must be kept current and accessible, serving as the authoritative reference for LDAP implementors. By specifying these procedures, the RFC ensures that LDAP can evolve in an organized manner: developers know what policy applies to their feature, IANA has clear guidance on approvals, and interoperability is maintained because assignments are centralized, documented, and stable.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are adding a feature to LDAP, you ask IANA for a number using the right process. If you are registering something common, you need more approvals. If it is experimental or private, you use special prefixes that do not need registration.
